title: Ephemeral socket leak -> node throttle postmortem
body:
Summary:

Nov 6 incident: ~08:10–09:40 UTC a subset (~12/120) of Frontier region edge nodes began rejecting new pod starts and showed increased pod restart rates. Symptoms: high kubelet CPU, slow container creation, kube-scheduler backpressure (Pending pods), and elevated 4xx/5xx for some customer control-plane calls. No data plane traffic loss for running pods; new workloads could not start.

Impact level:
- Partial region outage for new deployments in Frontier (customers saw errors when cluster autoscaler tried to add capacity and when CI jobs scheduled).
- No persistent tenant data loss.

What happened (short):
A kernel-level accumulation of ephemeral TCP socket entries on edge nodes exhausted ephemeral port/socket table (notably on nodes with heavy short-lived control-plane connections from the node-local CNI plugin and healthcheck sidecars). This manifested as kubelet churn when attempting to create new containers (docker/containerd could not bind ephemeral ports reliably), leading to container start failures and kube-scheduler pending queues. The root trigger appears to be a recent CNI health-probe change that increased connect frequency + a regression in a sidecar library that left sockets in TIME_WAIT longer than usual.

Timeline (best-effort):
- 08:07 UTC: Canary alert - autoscaler saw failures in pod creation (alert: cluster.autoscaler.create_failures).
- 08:10 UTC: Oncall paged (Priya). Initial triage: only Frontier edge nodes showing elevated kubelet CPU.
- 08:15 UTC: Observed spikes in node ephemeral socket counts (metrics: node.net.sockets.total) and conntrack table entries.
- 08:20 UTC: Mitigation: scaled down offending DaemonSet sidecar frequency by changing env var via emergency kustomize overlay on 12 nodes.
- 08:30 UTC: Applied temporary sysctl tweaks to free ephemeral range on two worst nodes (net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range widened) and cleared conntrack on the most impacted nodes.
- 08:45 UTC: Pod creation rate improved; kube-scheduler Pending queue reduced but some older pods remained in CrashLoopBackoff.
- 09:00 UTC: Confirmed upstream PR in CNI repo reverting aggressive probe rate.
- 09:30 UTC: Region declared recovered for customer-facing traffic; follow-up change scheduled.

Evidence and key metrics:
- Node-level sockstat at worst point (example):
  - TCP: inuse 16384 orphan 0 tw 24576 alloc 49152 mem 2048
  - /proc/net/sockstat showed huge tw counts for affected nodes (20–30k) vs healthy nodes (<500)
- conntrack entries: 45k on affected nodes; normal baseline ~1.5k
- kubelet CPU: 200–280% on affected nodes (multi-core) vs baseline 40–70%
- Container create latency: median 120ms -> 2.3s, P95 300ms -> 9s on affected nodes
- pod startup failures: ~18% of new pods on edges during window
- Logs: repeated "bind: cannot assign requested address" from container runtime around 08:12–08:28

Root cause hypothesis (single sentence):
A combined change (CNI health probe frequency increase + sidecar library regression) caused an unusually high rate of short-lived outbound connections from node-local processes, filling ephemeral port/TW sockets and exhausting kernel tables used during container startup binding. When the kernel could not allocate ephemeral ports, containerd failed to bind outbound ephemeral ports for container init, causing create/start failures and scheduler backpressure.

Why this escaped detection: 
- We did not have an alert specifically for rapid TW socket accumulation (we monitor conntrack entries and general net metrics, but thresholds were too permissive for short spikes).
- The change matrix crossed a threshold only on edge nodes with fleet-specific NAT/firewall behavior that prolonged TIME_WAIT entries.

Immediate mitigations taken (ordered):
1) Emergency config change to sidecar probe interval for the DaemonSet (rolled to 12 impacted nodes) — immediate reduction in connection churn.
2) conntrack -F on the worst 3 nodes after draining non-critical pods (risk accepted during incident window).
3) Temporarily broadened node ephemeral port range via sysctl to allow re-binding while longer-term changes deployed.
4) Reboot of two nodes where kernel socket tables were thrashing despite conntrack clearing.

Why mitigations worked: reducing connection frequency lowered new TIME_WAIT arrivals; conntrack clearing freed table slots; expanding port range reduced collisions during peak.

Permanent fixes and follow-ups (owners & ETA):
- SRE: Add new alerting for rapid TIME_WAIT and ephemeral socket churn (SRE-1284) — owner: Priya — ETA: 2024-11-20.
- CNI team: Revert aggressive probe change and add canary test that simulates high-probe-rate scenarios on NAT'd nodes (linked PR merged) — owner: Diego — ETA: complete (PR merged 2024-11-10).
- Developer platform: Patch sidecar lib to reduce TIME_WAIT retention by enabling SO_REUSEADDR where appropriate + close sockets promptly — owner: Liam — ETA: 2024-11-18.
- Runtime team: Add containerd/kubelet logs correlation for "bind cannot assign" to surface earlier in alerting — owner: Sophie — ETA: 2024-11-22.

Runbook draft (for SRE oncall):
1) Alert fires: "node.ephemeral.twpike" or "conntrack.table.spike". Immediately check top 10 nodes by conntrack entries:
   - kubectl get nodes -l region=frontier -o name | xargs -n1 -P5 bash -c 'ssh node "$CONNTRACK_CHECK"'
   - Quick checks: ss -s; cat /proc/net/sockstat; conntrack -L | wc -l
2) If conntrack > 10k on nodes and pod create errors observed:
   - Reduce non-critical probe/sidecar frequency via emergency kustomize overlay to the DaemonSet and roll to affected nodes.
   - If still degraded, clear conntrack on most impacted nodes after draining non-critical pods: "conntrack -F". Use with caution.
   - Expand ephemeral range: sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="1024 65535" (revert if undesirable).
   - If kernel shows thrash and conntrack -F not effective, schedule node reboot via cordon/drain + reboot.
3) Post-incident: collect netstat/ss output + /proc/net/sockstat + container runtime logs. Attach to SRE ticket.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why only the Frontier fleet exhibited such extreme TW retention compared to US/Europe fleets? (network NAT/timeouts config difference suspected)
- Did any customer workloads contribute increased short-lived connections coincidentally? We should correlate customer job schedules at 08:00–08:30.
- Should we introduce kernel-level tuning globally (reuseport/reuseaddr) or treat as fleet-specific?

Lessons learned:
- Short-lived, high-frequency connection patterns can be as disruptive as CPU/memory pressure; we lack fine-grained socket life-cycle alerting today.
- Small software changes (probe frequency) combined with infra quirks (NAT timeouts) can produce non-linear failures; we need better canarying across different fleet network topologies.
- Runbooks must include safe conntrack clearing guidance and per-fleet port-range recommendations.

Artifacts collected:
- node-logs.tgz (kubelet + containerd + system logs) uploaded to SRE ticket JIRA-SRE-1284
- conntrack-dumps for three nodes attached to Confluence link above

Immediate action items (short list):
- [Priya] Create alert and dashboard for TIME_WAIT/SPAWN socket churn — due 2024-11-20.
- [Diego] Confirm CNI probe revert is deployed across all fleets and add canary tests for NAT'd nodes — done for Frontier, confirm for others by 2024-11-13.
- [Liam] Prepare library patch and release plan for sidecar fix; coordinate with platform for rollout — due 2024-11-18.
- [SRE] Add explicit guidance in oncall runbook for safe use of conntrack -F and when to reboot.

Notes to self / rough debugging commands used during incident (copy/paste friendly):
- ss -s
- cat /proc/net/sockstat; cat /proc/net/sockstat6
- conntrack -L | wc -l; conntrack -S
- sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range
- journalctl -u kubelet --since "2024-11-06 07:50" | grep -E "bind: cannot assign|starting container"

Slack refs during incident: #oncall-frontier, thread ts 170981... (see linked artifacts)

If you have additional datapoints (customer job schedules, NAT config for Frontier) paste them here and I'll attach to the ticket. This doc is a working draft for the postmortem; once follow-ups are closed we should publish a trimmed final version to Confluence.
